description: We're Team SOL, a group of high school students from Nepal united by our curiosity for science, technology, and the universe. We love asking questions, exploring ideas, and challenging ourselves to turn what we learn into something meaningful. We're still learning and figuring things out, but that's what makes this journey exciting. For us, NASA Space Apps is more than a competition; it's a chance to explore, create, and be part of something bigger than ourselves.
summary:
Around the world, hundreds of millions of small farms face the same decision every year, with one try and no undo: what to plant next. Khet Sathi (खेत साथी, “field friend”) gives every farmer more than one try.

Built on NASA Earth observation that covers almost all of the world’s farmland (GPM IMERG precipitation, NASA POWER meteorology, Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2 greenness, NASADEM terrain, SMAP soil moisture, GRACE-FO groundwater and NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections), it creates a digital twin of a single field. A daily FAO-56 soil-water and yield-response model replays every crop rotation through 24 historical seasons, revealing which plan holds up in good years and hard ones. A prototype ESP32 soil probe checks each part of the field, and a Kalman update fuses its readings with the satellite estimate.

We built it first for a real farm in Bhaktapur, Nepal. There we found and corrected a 2017 step in NASA’s rain record, when far fewer ground gauges fed into it, and the same pipeline already runs for a field in Madagascar. Every answer comes in seven languages, labelled as checked, an estimate or not yet verifiable. Free, serverless, and made to travel.
details:
What it does
Khet Sathi (खेत साथी, “field friend”) is a free web app that helps small farmers decide what to grow next and what to watch out for. A farmer sees their field from above, how each part of its soil is doing, what to grow in the next three and six months, and what each month’s weather usually brings, with a “watch out” and a “do this”. It was built first for a real farm in Bhaktapur, Nepal, and works in seven languages.

How it works

  1. The field and its parts. An open drone map of a real farm in Kharipati, Bhaktapur (Rabi Shrestha, OpenAerialMap, CC-BY 4.0) gives the field’s outline. Our own drone isn’t built yet; this map stands in for it. Our code splits the field into 9 parts about 10 m across.
  2. NASA data for that field. Rain (GPM IMERG), weather (NASA POWER), greenness and growing seasons (HLS), elevation (NASADEM), soil moisture (SMAP, GLDAS), groundwater (GRACE-FO) and climate projections (NEX-GDDP-CMIP6), downloaded only for the area around the field. We downloaded only what we needed: small cut outs around our fields, not whole global files. That kept the data to a few gigabytes instead of hundreds, so the whole pipeline runs on an ordinary laptop.
  3. A copy of the field. A daily soil-water model based on FAO-56, with FAO’s yield-response method, replays every crop rotation through 24 past seasons (2002–2025) and counts how often each beats the current plan. If none usually does better, the app says “keep growing” instead of pushing a change.
  4. The ground. A prototype soil probe checks each part of the field. A Kalman update combines its reading with the satellite estimate, and a heatmap colours each tested part from dry to wet. Until the probe is calibrated against weighed soil, it compares the parts with each other.
  5. Simple answers. What to grow and when, how fast the soil dries in sun and wind, weather watch-outs, and a 24-year soil heatmap. A “Food and sprays” card sends farmers to their agriculture office for fertilizer amounts, notes that rice after lentil may need less urea (an estimate), and says to use only registered sprays, with no product names or doses. Every answer is labelled as checked, an estimate or not yet verifiable.

What we found
NASA’s IMERG rain record for our valley steps up by about 1.5 times from 2017, when far fewer ground gauges feed into it. We confirmed the change with independent rain data and corrected for it before using the rain.

Benefits
A farmer gets one try a year. Khet Sathi shows how each plan would have done in 24 past seasons on their own field, suggests trying a change in one part first, and warns before frost, heat and dry spells. It is free, needs no account, keeps the farmer’s answers on their phone, and works offline after the first visit.

Intended impact
More food from the same land, through fewer failed seasons and fewer empty months; healthier soil, kept covered and fed by lentil; and farmers better prepared for the weather. Because it uses only global, freely available NASA data, a field almost anywhere can be prepared on a laptop in a few hours. It already runs for a field in Madagascar. We plan to reach farmers through cooperatives and agriculture advisers, not only through phones.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (the app), Python (the data pipeline), C++ with Arduino (the probe).
  • Software: Leaflet for the map; NumPy, pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn, rasterio, h5py, pyet, earthaccess, pymannkendall and ruptures for the data and statistics; over 1,600 automated tests with pytest. Hosted as static files on Vercel, with no server.
  • Hardware (prototype): an ESP32 microcontroller with a capacitive soil-moisture sensor and a DS18B20 temperature sensor, programmed with Arduino using the OneWire and DallasTemperature libraries. It sends readings over USB to a small Python bridge that waits for each reading to settle and rejects unsteady ones. It is carried by hand today.

What makes it creative
It gives a farmer 24 tries instead of one, by replaying every crop plan through the past on their own field. It shows space and ground working together: the satellite guesses, the probe checks, and the app shows how sure it becomes. It checked NASA’s own rain record before trusting it. And it runs as plain files with no server, so it costs nothing to keep online.

Factors we considered

  • Trust: every answer says how sure we are, and ends with “you know your land best”.
  • Safety: no pesticide doses, and fertilizer amounts left to agriculture offices, since the government now sets them by soil.
  • Access: seven languages, Nepali months for Nepal, simple screens with symbols, low-cost phones and weak signal.
  • Privacy: no accounts, and answers stay on the phone.
  • Climate: a 2040 outlook from 23 climate models.
  • Honesty about limits, below.

Limits and next steps
No farmer has tested it yet, and most advice is labelled an estimate. The probe isn’t calibrated yet. Today, our team prepares each new field on a laptop. Next: a season of testing with farmers through a cooperative; farmers adding their own field’s location and photo in the app; our own drone to map each farm; a robot that carries the probe; preparing a whole valley in advance; more crops (pea and cabbage first); the government’s soil-based fertilizer rates; a printable page for advisers; local radio and SMS; and a nutrient sensor on the probe.

Use of AI
We used AI tools as assistants. Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote most of the code to our specifications, and we reviewed it and tested it with over 1,600 automated and manual tests. We reviewed our science ourselves, with help from Claude Fable, and Perplexity helped us find sources, which we then checked. Rishit designed the interface in Figma, using Claude Design for glass effects. Some illustrations in the app were drawn with AI assistance. Text in the five extra languages was drafted with AI and is awaiting native-speaker review. Every AI contribution is logged in our repository.

Team
Soren: team lead and full-stack development: the data pipeline, the science decisions and the app.
Rishit: UI design, in Figma. Along with Data accuracy and research
Vision: robotics: built and programmed the soil probe; reviewed the Nepali.
Pratik: front end and research; reviewed the Nepali.
Sailesh: mentor.
